title: Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges: Working Principle, Types and Selection Guide
text:
Introduction: Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges Pressure  is one of the most important things we measure in industries. Whether it is in pipelines, boilers, or machines, knowing the exact pressure helps keep operations safe and efficient. 
 One of the oldest and most trusted devices for this is the  Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge .
 Patented in 1849 by Edward Bourdon, this gauge quickly became popular because of its simplicity, accuracy, and reliability. 
 Even today, most mechanical dial-type pressure gauges you see work on the Bourdon tube principle.
 In this article, we will go step by step to understand its types, construction, working, advantages, disadvantages and uses  all in very simple words.
 How Does Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges Work?
 Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge animation. Numbered parts: C shaped Bourdon tube
 Socket (process connection)
 Link from tube tip
 Sector gear and pinion
 Pointer
 Dial
 Change the values yourself in the interactive Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge simulator . At the heart of the instrument is a curved, hollow metal tube . This tube is sealed at one end and connected to the pressure source at the other. When pressure enters the tube, it tries to straighten out.
 This movement is very small, but it is cleverly connected to a pointer mechanism. As the tube moves, the pointer moves across a dial, showing the pressure reading.
 Think of it like blowing air into a flattened straw. The straw tries to return to its round shape. The Bourdon tube Pressure Gauges works in a similar way!
 Materials used: Brass, phosphor bronze, or beryllium copper are common.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Types of Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Over time, different shapes of the tube were developed to handle different pressure ranges and applications. The three main types are:
 1. C-Type Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge
 Has a C-shaped tube . 
 Expands or contracts depending on pressure. 
 Best for low to medium pressure measurement. 
 This is the most common and widely used type. 
 Tip: If you see a standard pressure gauge in daily use, it is most likely a C-type Bourdon gauge.
 2. Spiral-Type Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge
 The tube is shaped like a spiral . 
 Provides better sensitivity and accuracy than C-type. 
 Mainly used for lower pressure ranges where fine accuracy is needed. 
 3. Helical-Type Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge
 Has a helix (spring-like) shape . 
 Can handle very high pressures safely. 
 Offers increased accuracy and resists damage from overpressure. 
 Tip: Use spiral type for better accuracy at low pressure, and helical type when dealing with very high pressure.
 
 Dry vs. Wet Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Bourdon gauges are also classified as dry or liquid-filled (wet) .
 Dry Gauge
 No liquid inside the case. 
 Works directly with the tube’s movement. 
 Simple and cost-effective. 
 Best for places with steady pressure and low vibration. 
 Wet (Liquid-Filled) Gauge
 Filled with glycerin or silicone oil. 
 The liquid acts like a cushion, damping vibrations and pulsations . 
 Gives more stable and accurate readings . 
 Perfect for pumps, compressors, and heavy-duty machinery. 
 Tip: If your gauge is in a vibrating environment, always go for a liquid-filled Bourdon gauge. It will last longer and show steady readings.
 Advantages of Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Simple design – Easy to use, no skilled operator required.

 Wide range – Can measure both low and very high pressures.

 No electricity needed – Works mechanically.

 Reliable accuracy – Suitable for real-time monitoring.

 Affordable and long-lasting – Costs less than many modern gauges.

 Disadvantages of Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Sensitive to vibration and shocks – Especially in dry types.

 Low displacement at tube end – Needs amplification for pointer movement.

 Hysteresis effect – Small errors may occur when pressure increases and decreases repeatedly.

 Tip: If accuracy is critical in vibrating conditions, use a liquid-filled gauge or go for electronic pressure transmitters.
 Common Uses of Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Measuring pressure of gases and liquids in pipelines. 
 Used in analog pressure meters . 
 Widely applied in the petroleum, chemical, and power industries . 
 Found in compressors, pumps, and hydraulic systems. 
 Construction of a Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge
 Tube Shape: Usually C-shaped, but can also be spiral or helical. 
 Fixed End: Connected to the pressure source. 
 Free End: Moves slightly when pressure is applied. 
 Linkage Mechanism: Transfers tube movement to the pointer. 
 Pointer and Dial: Shows the pressure reading. 
 The tube’s cross-section is not round but elliptical . When pressure enters, the tube tends to become circular. This causes the tube to straighten, and the free end moves. The pointer mechanism magnifies this movement into a readable scale.
 Tip: Even though the tube moves only about ⅛ inch, the clever linkage makes the pointer move across the entire dial!
 Working Principle of Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauge
 Pressure enters the tube.

 The tube tries to straighten.

 The free end of the tube moves.

 A linkage converts this small movement into rotation.

 The pointer shows the pressure on the dial.

 That’s it! Very simple and effective.
 Why Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges Are Still Popular
 Even after more than 170 years, Bourdon gauges are still widely used. Here’s why:
 Rugged and durable – Can last for years with minimal care. 
 Wide measuring range – From very low to extremely high pressures (0.6 to 7,000 bar). 
 Independent of power supply – Works even in remote areas without electricity. 
 Proven technology – Trusted by industries worldwide. 
 Practical Tips for Using Bourdon Tube Pressure Gauges
 Always check the pressure range before using a gauge. Don’t exceed its limit. 
 If the gauge will face pulsations , use a liquid-filled type. 
 Install gauges vertically for best accuracy.
